meta.title: Who really said "For truth and duty it is ever the fitting time; who waits until circumstances completely favor his undertaking, will never accomplish anything"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Martin Luther. The line traces to the theologian J. E. Huther, quoted in an 1868 Bible commentary. The "truth and duty" wording credited to Luther appears by 1891.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For truth and duty it is ever the fitting time; who waits until circumstances completely favor his undertaking, will never accomplish anything'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Luther. A Huther/Luther name mix-up: the line comes from J. E. Huther's comment on 2 Timothy, printed in an 1868 commentary and credited to Luther by 1876.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther — actually Johann Eduard Huther
answer.sourceLine: The line began as a comment by the 19th-century German theologian J. E. Huther on 2 Timothy. In English it appears in an 1868 Bible commentary that credits it to “Huther.” Later writers swapped one letter and credited it to Luther, and an 1891 quotation dictionary expanded “truth” to “truth and duty.” (Quote Investigator ↗)

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: A Commentary on the Holy Scriptures (Lange), Vol. 8 — J. J. Van Oosterzee on the Second Epistle to Timothy, 4:2
From the German by E. A. Washburn & E. Harwood
1868, Charles Scribner, New York (p. 112, per Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt: Timothy should fulfil his calling, not indeed when the time was so inopportune that they could receive no benefit, but when to himself it might be inconvenient. “For the truth, it is ever the fitting time; who waits until circumstances completely favor his undertaking, will never accomplish anything, but will remain in inactivity;” Huther.
source.trailTitle: How the line moved from Huther to Luther
trail: 1868: Van Oosterzee’s commentary on 2 Timothy in Lange’s Commentary on the Holy Scriptures quotes “For the truth, it is ever the fitting time…” and credits “Huther.” Quote Investigator calls this the earliest English match it found. (scan ↗)
1876: Jesse Lyman Hurlbut’s Lesson Compend for 1877 prints the same sentence and credits it to “LU,” which the book’s table of abbreviations defines as Luther. (Quote Investigator ↗)

1881: Huther’s own commentary in English says it differently: “For the truth, the occasion is always seasonable. He who desires to wait until the occasion seem completely favourable for his work, will never find it.” (T. & T. Clark edition ↗)
1891: Tryon Edwards’s A Dictionary of Thoughts, under “Opportunity” (p. 389), prints the popular form, “For truth and duty it is ever the fitting time…”, signed “Luther.” (scan ↗)
source.excerptNote: There is no “and duty” here, and the credit goes to “Huther,” not Luther. Quote Investigator transcribes the verb as “wait”; the Internet Archive scan reads “waits.”

sourceLink.text: Lange's Commentary, 1868 volume with Van Oosterzee on Timothy (Internet Archive)

source.rightsNote: Every documented form of this line comes from a 19th-century book published long before 1931: the 1868 English translation in Lange’s Commentary, Huther’s own 1881 English handbook, and the 1891 “truth and duty” wording in Tryon Edwards’s A Dictionary of Thoughts. All three are in the US public domain.

author.name: Johann Eduard Huther
author.heading: About Johann Eduard Huther
author.metaLine: 1807–1880 · German theologian, pastor & New Testament commentator
author.bio: Johann Eduard Huther was a 19th-century German theologian and pastor at Wittenförden, near Schwerin. He wrote the volume on the Pastoral Epistles (1 and 2 Timothy and Titus) in Heinrich Meyer’s Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament, which T. & T. Clark published in English in 1881. His remark that for the truth “it is ever the fitting time” was quoted in English Bible commentary and then credited to the far more famous Luther.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: The line has been credited to three people. Only one wrote it, and the most famous of them comes from a one-letter mix-up.

items.why: Quote Investigator puts this down to confusing the names “Huther” and “Luther.” The Luther credit appears in Hurlbut’s 1876 lesson book (as “LU”) and in The Spirit of Missions in 1887. Tryon Edwards’s 1891 Dictionary of Thoughts then fixed it in the quotation books, with “and duty” added (1891 scan ↗). No Luther text has been found. (Quote Investigator ↗)

Charles R. Hambly’s 1897 dental-practice manual, The Practice Builder, gives the second half of the line as a saying of Confucius. Quote Investigator calls this a surprising credit and finds nothing to support it. (Quote Investigator ↗)
The Dutch commentator printed the earliest English version Quote Investigator found, but he quoted it and named “Huther” as its source. (1868 scan ↗)

misattribution.truthLine: The thought comes from Johann Eduard Huther, who was commenting on Paul’s charge to Timothy to preach whether or not the moment seems right. The original line had only “truth”; “and duty” and the Luther credit were added later. (Quote Investigator ↗)

context.heading: Why the mix-up stuck
lead: Huther wrote the sentence as Bible commentary on 2 Timothy 4:2, where Paul tells Timothy to preach the word. Huther read the verse as being about the hearers’ situation, “whether the time seems to thee seasonable or unseasonable for it,” and added that for the truth the occasion is always seasonable (1881 English edition ↗).

Taken out of that technical setting, the sentence reads like a general call to act now, and readers who saw “Huther” easily took it for the far better-known reformer. Once the 1891 Dictionary of Thoughts printed it with “and duty” and a Luther credit, later quotation books copied that version (Quote Investigator ↗).
detailsBody: Quote Investigator believes Huther first wrote the remark in German, but it does not quote the German original, and this page has not located it either. The two English versions (1868 and 1881) are separate translations of the same idea.
context.pull: For the truth, the occasion is always seasonable.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI: the Luther credit is flawed; the line comes from Johann Eduard Huther through a Huther/Luther name mix-up; earliest English match 1868 (Lange/Van Oosterzee); Hurlbut 1876 'LU'; Spirit of Missions 1887; Edwards 1891 adds 'truth and duty'; Hambly 1897 credits Confucius; 'truth and duty' was a later elaboration

The 1868 Lange volume (Scribner, New York) contains 'For the truth, it is ever the fitting time; who waits until circumstances completely favor his undertaking, will never accomplish anything, but will remain in inactivity;' Huther, and names translators Washburn and Harwood (confirmed by full-text download)

Huther's 1881 T. & T. Clark English handbook contains 'For the truth, the occasion is always seasonable. He who desires to wait until the occasion seem completely favourable for his work, will never find it.' and the 'seasonable or unseasonable' gloss; catalog gives Huther's dates as 1807-1880

Tryon Edwards, A Dictionary of Thoughts (Cassell, 1891), under Opportunity, p. 389, prints 'For truth and duty it is ever the fitting time; who waits until circumstances completely favor his undertaking, will never accomplish anything. — Luther.'
Luther's Wikiquote page does not contain this line (raw wikitext searched for 'fitting time', 'Huther' and 'completely favor')
